To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the energy balance is sensitive to changes in surface albedo, surface temperature, and surface soil moisture; 2) the surface albedo, temperature, and surface moisture are sensitive to vegetation biomass and the amount of rainfall received; 3) surface albedo is sensitive to the amount of rainfall and the amount of vegetation biomass, and 4) surface albedo and surface moisture are related.

(1) remote sensing is useful for estimating surface soil moisture, vegetation biomass, surface albedo and temperature, and (2) remote sensing can improve the ability of models to compute fluxes of energy and moisture at the catchment scale.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new methodology for the estimation of energy and water fluxes at the land surface over semiarid rangleands using remote sensing.
the development and application of an interdisciplinary field study of the energy and water fluxes in the atmosphere-biosphere system over semiarid ranglelands.

the development of an integrated field program that will provide a comprehensive set of measurements to evaluate the effects of temporal variability in soil moisture on the surface energy and hydrologic balances.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of the remote sensing data in conjunction with other ground-based data has greatly enhanced our understanding of the energy and water fluxes in the atmosphere-biosphere system and the role of soil moisture and vegetation in controlling these fluxes.

the remote sensing measurements of surface soil water content, albedo, vegetation cover, and surface temperature are useful for estimating the energy and water fluxes in the atmosphere–biosphere system over rangelands.
the use of remote sensing data in biophysical models greatly enhances the ability of the models to compute fluxes over large areas and at different temporal scales.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the remote-sensing data were used to provide information on surface albedo, surface soil moisture, and vegetation cover and biomass.

we have demonstrated the feasibility of using remote-sensing data to provide measurements of the key factors controlling the surface energy budget and hydrological processes over semiarid ranglelands.

the use of remotely-sensed data for the estimation of land surface processes has proven to be a very valuable and promising technique for the study of hydrology, energy, and biophysical interactions in semiarid ranglelands.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the surface energy budget is highly sensitive to surface soil moisture.
remote sensing can provide a wealth of useful information about land surface processes.

the surface energy balance is very sensitive to the soil moisture and vegetation cover, and that the surface energy partitioning and the surface temperature is very dependent on the soil moisture and surface albedo.
